Migrating to synapser 3.0

2026-10-02

migration_to_synapser_3_0.Rmd

Who this guide is for

You need this guide if you have R code written against synapser 2.x. 3.0 is not a drop-in upgrade: function names, argument names, and the shape of the objects you get back have all changed, so an existing script will stop at its first Synapse call.

The failures are at least loud rather than silent — you’ll see could not find function "synTableQuery", unused argument (parentId = "syn123"), or AttributeError: 'File' object has no attribute 'properties' — and the fixes are mechanical once you know the four patterns below.

If you’re writing new code rather than porting old code, you don’t need this guide at all: start from Data Upload, Download, and Delete and Tables.

Why upgrade now

Staying on 2.x costs you more than the new API:

  • Frozen R dependencies. 2.x pins reticulate to 1.25–1.28 and rjson to ≤ 0.2.21, which holds back every other project sharing your R library. 3.0 drops both ceilings.
  • A Python ceiling. 2.x supports only Python 3.9–3.11 (with old pandas and numpy caps). 3.0 supports Python 3.10–3.14 and sets up its Python dependencies through reticulate::py_require(), with no virtualenv to manage.
  • An old view of Synapse. 2.x bundles synapseclient 4.4.2; 3.0 tracks 4.14, and because its R layer is generated from the Python models, it keeps pace from here on.

Why this release is not backwards compatible

Previous versions of synapser wrapped a hand-curated subset of the Python client behind R-idiomatic function names and camelCase arguments. 3.0 upgrades the reticulate/rjson dependency and, to keep pace with the Python client’s newer synapseclient.models/synapseclient.operations architecture, generates the R layer directly from those Python OOP models instead of maintaining a separate hand-written wrapper. The result is an API that mirrors the Python client field-for-field, so most existing synapser scripts will need updates.

This guide covers the Project/Folder/File/Table workflow — the paths most scripts use. The same patterns apply to every other entity type (Dataset, Views, Evaluation, Team, Wiki, …); see the full reference for exact signatures.

What you gain in 3.0

Upgrading costs a round of script updates (see below), but it buys you real capability, not just a version bump:

  • No Python environment to manage, and no pinned dependencies. synapser sets up the Python client it needs the first time it loads, so there is no virtualenv to create, activate, or repair by hand. Its R dependencies (reticulate, rjson) are no longer held to old versions, so installing synapser doesn’t force older packages on the rest of your R library.
  • New functionality that 2.x simply didn’t have. Recursive synCopy()/synSyncFromSynapse()/synWalk(), hierarchy-wide synDeletePermissions()/synListAcl() with a dry_run preview, and JSON Schema binding/validation (synBindSchema(), synValidateSchema(), …) are all new in 3.0 — see New in 3.0: capabilities that didn’t exist before below. None of these required someone to hand-port them from the Python client; they came along for free with the switch to generating the R layer directly from synapseclient.models.
  • New entity types, not just new methods on the old ones. VirtualTable, DatasetCollection, Agent/AgentSession, and Organization/JSONSchema have no 2.x counterpart at all, and the view types (EntityView, MaterializedView, SubmissionView) replace 2.x’s EntityViewSchema/MaterializedViewSchema/SubmissionViewSchema while picking up the same column, query, and ACL verbs as Table.
  • Faster access to new Python client features going forward. Because the R layer is generated from the same OOP models the Python client ships, new methods and arguments added to synapseclient can be surfaced in R without waiting on a hand-written wrapper to catch up — which is how the gap above accumulated in the first place.
  • One mental model, matching the Python docs. Every entity — File, Folder, Table, Dataset, Project, … — now follows the same Constructor(...) |> synMethod(...) |> synStore() shape, with snake_case arguments that match the Python client’s field names exactly. If the R docs for a function are unclear, the Python reference describes the same method, argument for argument — that cross-reference didn’t reliably work in 2.x, where argument names and calling conventions were hand-curated per function.

In short, synapser 2.x emphasizes compatibility with an older hand-maintained API surface, while 3.0 trades one migration pass for long-term gains: fewer dependency constraints, broader Synapse coverage (new entities plus recursive and schema workflows), and an API that stays aligned with the actively evolving Python client instead of drifting behind it.

The rest of this guide covers what to change in existing scripts to get there.

Before you upgrade

synapser 3.0 requires:

  • R 4.2.0 or later.
  • reticulate 1.44.0 or later. Earlier versions, including the 1.28 that 2.x pinned, fail with could not find a Python environment for /.
  • Python 3.10 to 3.14, only if you point synapser at a Python you manage yourself. Otherwise reticulate downloads a compatible Python and the Synapse Python client into a managed environment the first time synapser loads.

If you set up pinned dependencies for 2.x (such as rjson and reticulate), remove them, and remove the r-reticulate virtualenv and any RETICULATE_PYTHON setting so synapser can use its managed environment via uv. Then restart R:

install.packages(c("rjson", "reticulate"))
reticulate::virtualenv_remove("r-reticulate")

Run reticulate::py_config() to check which Python synapser is using. See Installation for details.

Four patterns to relearn

1. Instance-first, then pipe

Every entity is now a real object you construct directly — File(...), Folder(...), Table(...), Project(...), … — and every operation on it is a “verb” function (synStore(), synGet(), synSetProperties(), synAddColumn(), synDeleteRows(), …) that takes the instance as its first argument. You construct the object first, then thread it through a chain of these verbs with the native pipe, tidyverse-style, instead of reassigning a variable at every step:

# 2.x -- synStore() was one Python-backed function shared by every entity
# type, with Python duck-typing on `obj` internally; each step reassigned a
# variable rather than chaining
file <- File(path, parentId = "syn123")
file <- synStore(file)
file <- synGet(file$properties$id, downloadFile = FALSE)

# 3.0 -- construct the instance, then pipe it through verbs
file <- File(path = path, parent_id = "syn123") |>
  synStore() |>
  synGet(file_options = FileOptions(download_file = FALSE))

This is the change everything else in this guide follows from. Two kinds of function take an instance this way:

  • synStore(), synGet(), and synDelete() are single factory functions that accept any supported entity — or, for synGet() and synDelete(), a Synapse ID string instead — and apply the behavior appropriate to that entity’s type.
  • Every other verb (synAddColumn(), synGetAcl(), synCopy(), synWalk(), synBindSchema(), …) is a generic that dispatches on the class of the object you pipe in. The same verb name therefore works uniformly across every entity type that supports it, instead of each operation being its own hand-written function reconciling the differences between entity types internally.

2. Properties are no longer nested under $properties and synSetProperties

Properties and annotations are now plain fields on the object. Read them directly, and update them with the convenience function synSetProperties(), which sets any number of fields, including annotations, in one call and returns the entity so you can pipe it into synStore():

# 2.x
entity$properties$id
entity$properties$name
entity$annotations$assay

# 3.0
entity$id
entity$name
entity$annotations$assay

synGet(synapse_id) |>
  synSetProperties(
    name = "new name",
    version_label = "2",
    annotations = list(assay = "RNA-seq")
  ) |>
  synStore()

Setting annotations replaces all of the entity’s existing annotations. To add to them instead, combine them first: synSetProperties(annotations = append(entity$annotations, list(key = "value"))).

3. Arguments are snake_case, matching the Python client exactly 

# 2.x
synGet(entity, downloadFile = FALSE)
synStore(obj, forceVersion = FALSE, versionLabel = "2")
File(path, parentId = project$properties$id)

# 3.0
synGet(entity, file_options = FileOptions(download_file = FALSE))

Some arguments moved rather than just changed case. Options that 2.x passed to synStore() — forceVersion, versionLabel — are fields on the entity itself in 3.0 (force_version, version_label), set at construction or with synSetProperties(). synStore() itself takes only the entity, an optional parent, and the per-type option objects (StoreFileOptions(), StoreContainerOptions(), StoreTableOptions(), …); there is no force_version argument on it.

4. Mutation goes through synSetProperties(), then an explicit synStore()

Directly assigning into $properties no longer works. Properties are set with synSetProperties() — which validates the field names against the object’s dataclass fields — and piped into synStore():

# 2.x
entity$properties$name <- "new name"
entity <- synStore(entity)

# 3.0
entity <- synGet(synapse_id) |>
  synSetProperties(name = "new name") |>
  synStore()

Table columns are the one exception — those are still mutated in place on the $columns list before synStore():

table$columns[["Expression"]]$name <- "Expression2"
table$columns[["Expression"]]$column_type <- "INTEGER"
table |> synStore()

The column verbs synAddColumn(), synDeleteColumn(), and synReorderColumn() work the same way: they change the table object in place and return nothing, so they are separate statements rather than links in a pipe into synStore():

table |> synAddColumn(Column(name = "Expression", column_type = "STRING"))
table |> synStore()

Side-by-side reference: common operations

Task 2.x (legacy) 3.0 (new)
Create + store an entity File(path, parentId = "syn123") then synStore(obj) File(path = path, parent_id = "syn123") \|> synStore()
Suppress a new version synStore(obj, forceVersion = FALSE) File(path = path, parent_id = "syn123", force_version = FALSE) \|> synStore()
Set name / version label entity$properties$name <- "x"; synStore(entity) synGet(id) \|> synSetProperties(name = "x") \|> synStore()
Move an entity synMove(entity, newParent) synGet(id) \|> synSetProperties(parent_id = "syn456") \|> synStore()
Track provenance synStore(obj, used = "syn123", executed = "syn456") synGet(id) \|> synSetProperties(activity = Activity(used = list(UsedEntity(target_id = "syn123")), executed = list(UsedEntity(target_id = "syn456")))) \|> synStore()
Remove provenance synDeleteProvenance(entity) synDisassociateActivityFromEntity(Activity, parent = entity)
Get an entity synGet(entity, ...) synGet(synapse_id, file_options = FileOptions(...))
Get a specific version synGet(entity, version = 1) synGet(synapse_id, version_number = 1L)
Skip downloading file content synGet(entity, downloadFile = FALSE) synGet(synapse_id, file_options = FileOptions(download_file = FALSE))
Delete a version only synDelete(obj, version = 1) synDelete(entity, version = 1L, version_only = TRUE)
Query a table synTableQuery(sql) synQuery(sql)
Create a table column synCreateColumn(name = "x", columnType = "STRING") Column(name = "x", column_type = "STRING")
Add a table column manual list manipulation table \|> synAddColumn(Column(name = "x", column_type = "STRING")), then table \|> synStore()
Remove a table column manual list manipulation table \|> synDeleteColumn(name = "x"), then table \|> synStore()
Insert-or-update table rows query, merge, re-store table \|> synUpsertRows(values = df, primary_keys = list("Name"))
Build a table from a CSV, inferring columns synBuildTable(name, parent, "genes.csv") Table(name = ..., parent_id = ...) \|> synStore() \|> synStoreRows(values = "genes.csv", schema_storage_strategy = "INFER_FROM_DATA")

Removed functions

Because 3.0 generates the R layer from the Python models, a 2.x function survives only if the models expose an equivalent. These are the removals most scripts will hit.

Renamed or restructured

  • synBuildTable() → Table(...) |> synStore() |> synStoreRows(values = ..., schema_storage_strategy = "INFER_FROM_DATA"). The table has to exist before rows can be stored into it, so the synStore() step is not optional.
  • synTableQuery() → synQuery()
  • synMove() → synSetProperties(parent_id = ...) |> synStore()
  • synGetChildren() → synSyncFromSynapse(recursive = FALSE, download_file = FALSE) and then the container’s $files/$folders, or synWalk() to traverse a whole tree
  • synGetAnnotations() / synSetAnnotations() → the annotations field: read entity$annotations, write synSetProperties(annotations = list(...)) |> synStore()
  • synGetProvenance() / synSetProvenance() / synDeleteProvenance() / synUpdateActivity() → the activity field (an Activity() object) set via synSetProperties(), and synDisassociateActivityFromEntity(Activity, parent = entity) to remove it
  • synCreateColumn() / synCreateColumns() / synGetColumn() / synGetColumns() / synGetTableColumns() → the Column() constructor and the table’s own $columns list
  • synCreateSnapshotVersion() → synSnapshot()
  • synRestGET() / synRestPOST() / synRestPUT() / synRestDELETE(), and the 2.x synRestGetAsync() family → synRestGet(), synRestPost(), synRestPut(), synRestDelete()
  • synCreateTeam() → Team(name = "...") |> synCreate(); synGetTeam() → Team |> synGetFromId(id = id) or Team |> synGetFromName(name = name); synDeleteTeam() → synDelete(team)
  • synSendMembershipInvitation() → synInviteToTeam(); synGetTeamOpenInvitations() → synGetOpenInvitations(); synGetMembershipStatus() → synGetUserMembershipStatus()
  • synGetUserProfile() → UserProfile |> synGetFromId(user_id = user_id) or UserProfile |> synGetFromUsername(username = username)
  • Wikis: synGetWiki() → WikiPage(owner_id = ..., id = ...) |> synGet(); storing a wiki page → WikiPage(owner_id = ..., title = ..., markdown = ...) |> synStore(); synGetWikiHeaders() → as.list(WikiHeader() |> synGet(owner_id = ...)); synGetWikiAttachments() → synGetAttachmentHandles(), or synGetAttachment() to fetch one attachment. See Wikis.
  • Evaluations: synGetEvaluation() → Evaluation(id = ...) |> synGet(); synGetEvaluationByName() → Evaluation(name = ...) |> synGet(); synGetEvaluationByContentSource() → synGetEvaluationsByProject(project_id = ...). See Evaluation.
  • Submissions: synSubmit() → Submission(entity_id = ..., evaluation_id = ...) |> synStore(); synGetSubmission() → Submission(id = ...) |> synGet(); synGetSubmissionStatus() → SubmissionStatus(id = ...) |> synGet(), then synStore() to update it; synGetSubmissions() → Submission() |> synGetEvaluationSubmissions(evaluation_id = ...); synGetSubmissionBundles() → SubmissionBundle() |> synGetEvaluationSubmissionBundles(evaluation_id = ...). See Submission.
  • Storage locations: synCreateS3StorageLocation() / synCreateStorageLocationSetting() → StorageLocation(...) |> synStore(); synGetMyStorageLocationSetting() → StorageLocation(storage_location_id = ...) |> synGet(); synSetStorageLocation(), synGetProjectSetting(), and synGetStsStorageToken() keep their names but are now verbs piped from a Folder or Project (folder |> synSetStorageLocation(storage_location_id = ...)).
  • Download lists: synGetDownloadList() → synDownloadListFiles(); synGetDownloadListManifest() → synDownloadListManifest(); synRemoveFromDownloadList() → synDownloadListRemove(); synClearDownloadList() → synDownloadListClear(). synDownloadListAdd() is new.

Note the calling convention in the Team and UserProfile entries. synGetFromId(), synGetFromName(), synGetFromUsername(), and synDisassociateActivityFromEntity() wrap Python classmethods, so their first argument is the constructor (Team, UserProfile, Activity) — that is what selects the implementation — rather than an instance of it. An empty instance works as the marker too (Team() |> synGetFromId(id = id)), which is the style the reference pages use.

Not currently exposed in 3.0

These 2.x functions have no model-layer equivalent yet. Until they get one, call the REST API directly with synRestGet()/synRestPost()/synRestPut()/synRestDelete(), or keep that step of the pipeline in the Python client:

  • File handles: synCreateExternalS3FileHandle(), synUploadFileHandle().
  • Other: synDownloadTableColumns(), synGetConfigFile(), synInvalidateAPIKey().

New in 3.0: capabilities that didn’t exist before

The OOP-model generation doesn’t just rename old functions — it also surfaces Python client functionality that synapser never exposed at all. These functions have no 2.x equivalent, so there’s nothing to migrate from, but existing scripts that worked around their absence (manual recursion to bulk update ACLs, hand-rolled directory walks, shelling out to synapseutils from Python) can now be simplified.

Richer access control

synDeletePermissions() and synListAcl() are new. Both work over a single entity or an entire container hierarchy at once, so an audit or cleanup that used to mean writing your own recursive walk over 2.x’s synGetChildren() — and getting the edge cases (nested folders, inherited vs. local ACLs) right yourself — is now one call. dry_run lets you preview exactly what a recursive permissions change will touch before anything is deleted, which matters once you’re operating on an entire project tree instead of a single entity:

# Preview, then perform, a recursive ACL cleardown of a folder and its children
Folder(id = "syn123") |> synDeletePermissions(recursive = TRUE, include_container_content = TRUE, dry_run = TRUE)
Folder(id = "syn123") |> synDeletePermissions(recursive = TRUE, include_container_content = TRUE)

# List every ACL in a hierarchy, optionally as an ASCII tree
Folder(id = "syn123") |> synListAcl(recursive = TRUE, log_tree = TRUE)

One semantic change on an existing function: synGetPermissions(instance) now always returns your own effective permissions — the old principalId argument is gone. To check another user or team’s permissions, use synGetAcl(instance, principal_id = ...) instead, which still supports it:

# 2.x -- check someone else's permissions
synGetPermissions(entity, principalId = "273948")

# 3.0 -- synGetPermissions() is caller-only; use synGetAcl() for another principal
synGet(synapse_id) |> synGetAcl(principal_id = 273948L)

Container traversal and sync

synapser never exposed synapseutils’ copy, syncFromSynapse, or walk utilities — getting this functionality previously meant dropping out of R into a Python script, or reimplementing the recursion (and its failure handling) by hand with repeated synGetChildren()/synGet() calls. In 3.0 they’re methods on any container object, so a bulk copy, a full local mirror of a project, or a metadata-only inventory of an entity tree is a single pipeline that stays in R:

# Recursively copy a folder, and everything in it, to a new parent
Folder(id = "syn123") |> synCopy(parent_id = "syn456")

# Recursively download a folder tree, populating $files/$folders/$tables/...
folder <- Folder(id = "syn123") |> synSyncFromSynapse(path = "~/local-copy")

# Traverse a hierarchy without downloading anything
for (entry in as.list(folder |> synWalk())) {
  dirpath <- entry[[1]]; dirs <- entry[[2]]; nondirs <- entry[[3]]
  cat(dirpath[[1]], "\n")
}

synWalk() returns a GeneratorWrapper — the same lazy-iterator object 2.x returned from synGetChildren(), which no longer exists. Call as.list() on it to materialize every result into a plain list, or nextElem() to pull results one at a time; you can’t loop over it directly the way you can a list. For the narrower job synGetChildren() used to do — listing one container’s immediate children without downloading them — use synSyncFromSynapse(recursive = FALSE, download_file = FALSE) and read the resulting $files/$folders.

JSON Schema binding and validation

Also new: entities can be bound to a JSON Schema and validated against it directly from R. This lets you enforce metadata/annotation standards on Files, Folders, and Tables as part of an R pipeline — catching entities with missing or malformed annotations programmatically instead of relying on manual review or the web UI — and derive annotation values automatically from the schema rather than entering them by hand:

folder <- Folder(id = "syn123")
folder |> synBindSchema(json_schema_uri = "myOrg-mySchema-0.0.1")
folder |> synValidateSchema()
folder |> synUnbindSchema()

synBindSchema() returns the binding record rather than the entity, so bind the schema as its own statement and keep piping the entity itself.

This applies to Files, Folders, Tables, Projects, and other container/entity types. Creating the organization and schema themselves uses the new Organization/JSONSchema constructors — see ?Folder_synBindSchema for a full example. The rest of the family: synGetSchema() and synGetSchemaDerivedKeys() on any bindable entity, plus synGetSchemaValidationStatistics() and synGetInvalidValidation() on containers (Folder, Project).

Known pitfall: integer literals

R’s bare numeric literals (1) are doubles. Parameters the Synapse API expects as integers — version_number, version, row IDs/versions in synDeleteRows(df = ...) — must use the L suffix (1L). Passing 1 instead of 1L can produce unexpected behavior or an API error. This isn’t new in 3.0, but it surfaces more often now that raw integer parameters are exposed directly instead of being hidden behind wrapper defaults.

Worked example: before and after 

# ---- 2.x ----
library(synapser)
synLogin()

project <- Project("My Project")
project <- synStore(project)

file <- File(path = "data.csv", parentId = project$properties$id)
file <- synStore(file)

file <- synGet(file$properties$id, downloadFile = FALSE)
file$annotations <- c(assay = "RNA-seq")
file <- synStore(file, forceVersion = FALSE)

synDelete(project)
# ---- 3.0 ----
library(synapser)
synLogin()

project <- Project(name = "My Project") |> synStore()

file <- File(path = "data.csv", parent_id = project$id) |> synStore()

file <- synGet(file$id, file_options = FileOptions(download_file = FALSE)) |>
  synSetProperties(annotations = list(assay = "RNA-seq"), force_version = FALSE) |>
  synStore()

synDelete(project)
